The **elements of music**: rhythm, melody/pitch, harmony/texture, dynamics, timbre (tone colour), form and tempo.

body: Folk songs pertain exclusively to the musics of Africa.

options.text: Folk song is an African ensemble

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Folk songs exist in **every culture** (European, Asian, American folk traditions), not only in Africa.

## Simplified explanation

Every culture has folk songs, so this is **not true**.

body: Music has a name across all African cultures.

options.text: There are words in every African community
The meaning is objective in cultural context

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Many African languages have **no single word equivalent to 'music'**: song, drumming and dance are named together as one performance (e.g. Akan _agorɔ_, 'play'). This is part of the 'problem of meaning' that leads scholars to speak of the **musical arts of Africa**.

## Simplified explanation

Many African languages have **no separate word** for music: not true.

body: Music, dance and drama are all terms for
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Because song, instruments, dance and drama are **integrated** in African performance, scholars (Nzewi, Nketia) use **'musical arts of Africa'** for the whole complex.

## Simplified explanation

Together they are the **musical arts of Africa**.

body: One of the following is an example of a **membranophone**:
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The **atumpan** (Akan talking drums) are membranophones. **Frikyiwa** (castanet) and bells are idiophones; 'a stretched membrane' is a description, not an instrument.

## Simplified explanation

The **atumpan** drum is a membranophone.

body: Which classification of instruments has the **widest variety** in Ghana?
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Idiophones** (bells, rattles, castanets, xylophones, clappers, stamping tubes, lamellophones) are the most varied and numerous instruments in Ghana and Africa (Nketia).

## Simplified explanation

**Idiophones** come in the most varieties.

body: Music instruments in Africa are not only used for music making. They are also used to communicate to both man and spirits.

options.text: African musicians do not deal with spirits

explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Instruments **talk** (atumpan drum language), **signal** (gong-gong announcements, horns), recite history and praise, and **invoke ancestors and deities** in rituals.

## Simplified explanation

Yes: African instruments **speak to people and spirits**.

body: One of the following is **not** a socio-economic benefit of the practice of African musics.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Socio-economic benefits include **tourism**, **commercialisation** (income, the music industry), **unity and community participation**, **cultural identity** and **research**. Dance groups meeting is merely an activity.

## Simplified explanation

Groups meeting is not a benefit in itself.

body: Which of the following is **not** part of the **Adowa** ensemble?
explanation:

The Adowa ensemble: **atumpan** (master drums), **apentemma**, **petia**, **dawuro** (bell) and other supporting drums. The other three options are core Adowa instruments.

## Simplified explanation

Atumpan, petia and dawuro are in Adowa; the odd one out is **adakapopron**.

**Gota** is not in the Agbadza ensemble.

explanation:

**Highlife** is a popular **neo-traditional/popular** African genre blending local rhythms and melodies with Western instruments: part of contemporary African musical arts and 'new trends'.

## Simplified explanation

Highlife **is** African music, so the statement is **not true**.

body: **Ubuntu** is a Zulu word which means

**Ubuntu** (Nguni) means **humanity (towards others)**: 'I am because we are' (_umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu_), stressing community, compassion and interconnectedness.

## Simplified explanation

Ubuntu means **humanity**.

body: One of the following is **not** a major element in the **musical arts of Africa**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The musical arts of Africa integrate **music, dance and drama** (plus visual arts such as costume). 'Mode of performance' describes how they are presented, not an art element.

## Simplified explanation

The main elements are music, dance and drama.

body: Distinguish between **occasional** and **incidental** music groupings, and discuss the **recreational** grouping.
answer:
> [!answer]
> - **Occasional music:** music performed for **specific social or ritual occasions and events**: festivals, funerals, installation of chiefs, rites of passage (e.g. Adowa at funerals, Dipo songs).
> - **Incidental music:** music that **accompanies other activities** and arises **incidentally** in the course of them: work songs, lullabies, children's game songs, storytelling songs.
> - **Recreational music:** music performed mainly for **entertainment and social enjoyment** in leisure time: Kpanlogo, Borborbor, Apatampa, Kpatsa.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These groupings (following Nketia) classify music by **context and function**, reflecting the integration of music into social life rather than separation as 'concert' art.

## Simplified explanation

**Occasional** music is for **special events**; **incidental** music goes along with **daily activities** like work; **recreational** music is for **fun**.

body: The **Hornbostel–Sachs** method is based on _______. **Group** the following instruments: kora, seperewa, dondo, kagan, mbira, atenteben, xylophone, odurugya. Critique the method.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Basis:** the **mode of sound production**: what vibrates to produce the sound.
>
> | Category | Instruments |
> |---|---|
> | **Chordophones** (strings) | kora, seperewa |
> | **Membranophones** (skins) | dondo, kagan |
> | **Idiophones** (body vibrates) | mbira, xylophone |
> | **Aerophones** (air) | atenteben, odurugya |
>
> **Critique:** it is **Western-derived and acoustic only**; it ignores **cultural meaning, function, symbolism and indigenous classification** systems (e.g. by gender, status, ritual use); some instruments are **hybrid** and hard to place; it needed later additions (electrophones).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

African societies have their own classifications, e.g. by **social role** (royal vs recreational), **gender** or **ensemble function** (master vs supporting). Nketia adapted Hornbostel–Sachs for African instruments while noting these limits.

## Simplified explanation

Instruments are grouped by **what vibrates**: strings (kora), skins (dondo), the body itself (mbira), or air (atenteben). The method ignores **culture and meaning**.

body: The **social learning theory** was proposed by _______. List **four characteristics** of the **master–apprenticeship** model.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Albert Bandura** (1977).
>
> **Master–apprentice characteristics:** learning by **observation and imitation** of a master musician · **oral/aural** transmission (no notation) · **long-term, hands-on** practice in real performance contexts · a **hierarchical** relationship with respect and discipline · **gradual progression** from simple to complex roles (supporting to master drum) · **feedback/correction** by the master · learning embedded in **community life**.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Bandura's theory explains learning through **attention, retention, reproduction and motivation** (modelling), which fits how apprentices learn traditional music by watching masters and practising in context.

## Simplified explanation

**Bandura** proposed social learning. Apprentices learn by **watching and copying a master**, by ear, through practice over time, and with corrections.

body: Define a **plot** and list the parts of a traditional plot. Distinguish between a **prop** and a **costume** as elements of drama.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Plot:** the **sequence of events** in a story or drama, organised to create conflict and resolution.
>
> **Parts (Freytag's pyramid):** **exposition** (introduction) → **rising action** (complication) → **climax** → **falling action** → **resolution/denouement**.
>
> **Prop vs costume:** a **prop** is a **movable object handled** by performers on stage (a sword, stool, fly whisk); a **costume** is the **clothing and accessories worn** by performers to portray a character.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

African storytelling and drama (e.g. Ananse stories, concert parties) often follow a similar arc but add **audience participation**, songs and interludes (mmoguo).

## Simplified explanation

A plot is the **story's order of events**: introduction, rising action, climax, falling action, ending. A **prop** is something carried; a **costume** is something worn.

body: List **four differences** between **traditional African music** and **Western art music**. Differentiate between **harmony** and **melody**. What is the difference between **cantor and chorus** and **call and response**?
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Differences:** African music is mainly **oral** and Western art music is **notated** · African is **communal and participatory** vs Western **performer–audience** separation · African music is **functional** (tied to social events) vs Western 'art for art's sake' in concerts · African has **complex polyrhythm** and **cyclic forms** vs Western emphasis on **harmony** and developmental forms · African **integrates dance and drama** · African uses **improvisation** more.
>
> **Melody** is a **succession of single notes** forming a tune (horizontal); **harmony** is the **simultaneous sounding** of different notes (chords) (vertical).
>
> **Call and response:** a leader's call is answered by a group response that **alternates** with it. **Cantor and chorus:** the chorus **overlaps or joins in** with the cantor (leader), or the cantor sings an extended solo and the chorus repeats a refrain. Both involve a leader and a group, but the **relationship and overlap** differ.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These contrasts are generalisations: African art music (Amu, Nketia) uses notation, and Western traditions include folk and participatory forms. Polyphony in African music often arises from **overlapping call and response** and **parallel motion** (e.g. in thirds, fourths).

## Simplified explanation

African music is usually **by ear, shared by all, and tied to events**, with **complex rhythms**; Western art music is **written down and performed for listeners**. Melody is a **tune**; harmony is **notes together**.

body: State **two importance** of **costume** in a dance, and explain **two factors** that account for the **differences** in African music.
answer:
> [!answer]
> **Costume:** **identifies** the dancers' roles, status or group · **enhances visual appeal** and spectacle · conveys **cultural meaning and symbolism** (colours: red and black for funerals) · accentuates **movement** (skirts, rattles) · may hold **ritual** significance.
>
> **Differences in African music:** **language** (tonal languages shape melody and drum language) · **ecology and environment** (available materials for instruments) · **religion and contact** (Islamic influence in the north; Christian and Western influence on the coast) · **social organisation** (centralised kingdoms with court music vs acephalous societies) · **occupation** (pastoral vs farming communities) · history and migration.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Africa's musical diversity reflects its **linguistic, ecological and historical** diversity: one reason scholars prefer the plural 'African musics'.

## Simplified explanation

Costumes **show who the dancers are**, look **beautiful** and carry **meaning**. African music differs because of **languages, environment, religion and history**.

body: Discuss the **socio-economic impacts** of the musical arts of Africa, based on: (i) tourism (ii) commercialisation (iii) cultural identity (iv) unity/community participation (v) research.
answer:
1. **Tourism:** festivals (Panafest, Homowo, Aboakyer, Chale Wote), dance performances and music heritage sites attract **local and foreign tourists**, generating revenue, jobs (guides, hotels, artisans) and foreign exchange; diaspora 'roots' tourism (Year of Return) features drumming and dance.
2. **Commercialisation:** music and dance become **products**: recordings, concerts, streaming, dance troupes for hire, sale of instruments and costumes, highlife/hiplife/Afrobeats industries; income for musicians, producers and craftsmen, with copyright royalties.
3. **Cultural identity:** music expresses and preserves **history, values, language and ethnic and national identity** (national anthems, Adowa at state functions); it builds pride and resists cultural imperialism.
4. **Unity/community participation:** communal performance brings people together across age, gender and status; it promotes **social cohesion**, conflict resolution and solidarity (the Ubuntu spirit); music mobilises for development and political campaigns.
5. **Research:** music is a field for **ethnomusicology, anthropology and education**; research documents and preserves traditions, informs curricula, and creates academic and archival employment.

> [!answer]
> Tourism (festivals, jobs, revenue), commercialisation (recordings, performances, industries, royalties), cultural identity (heritage, pride), unity and participation (cohesion, mobilisation), research (documentation, education, scholarship).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The **creative economy** is increasingly recognised in Africa's development agendas (UNESCO; Ghana's Creative Arts Agency). Commercialisation also raises concerns about authenticity, appropriation and fair pay to tradition-bearers.

## Simplified explanation

African music brings **tourists and money**, becomes a **business**, shows **who we are**, **unites communities**, and is studied in **research**.
hint: Take each heading in turn with Ghanaian examples.

body: Group the following into their **families of African instrument classification** (in a table): atenteben, gyile, banana bell, rattle, atumpan, djembe, kora, sogo, mbira, bell, umwironge, seperewa, adakapoprom, petia, donno, axatse, kidi, kagan.
answer:
| Idiophones | Membranophones | Chordophones | Aerophones |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gyile (xylophone) | Atumpan | Kora | Atenteben |
| Banana bell | Djembe | Seperewa | Umwironge (Rwandan flute) |
| Rattle | Sogo | | |
| Mbira | Adakapoprom | | |
| Bell (dawuro/gankogui) | Petia | | |
| Axatse | Donno (hourglass drum) | | |
| | Kidi | | |
| | Kagan | | |

_Basis:_ **idiophones** sound by the vibration of their own body; **membranophones** by a stretched skin; **chordophones** by strings; **aerophones** by a vibrating column of air.

> [!answer]
> Idiophones: gyile, banana bell, rattle, mbira, bell, axatse. Membranophones: atumpan, djembe, sogo, adakapoprom, petia, donno, kidi, kagan. Chordophones: kora, seperewa. Aerophones: atenteben, umwironge.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Two items on the original list are illegible in the scan and are omitted here. Note the dominance of **membranophones and idiophones** in West African ensembles; the **mbira** (thumb piano, a lamellophone) is an idiophone because its metal tongues vibrate.

## Simplified explanation

Sort by what vibrates: **bells, rattles, xylophone, mbira** (idiophones); **drums** (membranophones); **kora, seperewa** (strings); **atenteben, umwironge** (wind).
hint: Ask what vibrates for each instrument.

body: Discuss the **differences between African musics and Western music** based on: (i) texture (ii) dynamics (iii) pitch (iv) form (v) rhythm. _(Also: drawing on three characteristics, distinguish African indigenous and Western art musical forms.)_
answer:
| Element | African musics | Western (art) music |
|---|---|---|
| **Texture** | Mostly **polyphonic/polyrhythmic** layering: overlapping call and response, ostinato patterns, parallel thirds or fourths; dense layers of percussion | Often **homophonic** (melody + chords) or contrapuntal (fugue), based on **functional harmony** |
| **Dynamics** | Less written; changes arise **contextually** and through intensity of participation; often loud outdoor performance | **Notated** and carefully graded (pp to ff, crescendo, diminuendo) as an expressive device |
| **Pitch** | Influenced by **speech tones** of tonal languages; pentatonic, hexatonic and heptatonic scales; **non-fixed tuning** to community preference | **Fixed, standardised tuning** (A = 440 Hz), equal temperament, major/minor diatonic system |
| **Form** | **Cyclic, open, repetitive** forms (call and response, ostinato) with improvisation; length depends on the occasion | **Closed, through-composed** or sectional forms (sonata, rondo, binary/ternary); fixed length |
| **Rhythm** | **Polyrhythm and cross-rhythm**, a **timeline** (bell pattern) as reference, additive rhythms (3+3+2), complex interlocking | Mainly **divisive, metrical** rhythm in regular bars, one main meter at a time, with emphasis on melody and harmony |

**Other characteristics:** African musics are **oral, communal, functional and integrated** with dance and drama; Western art music is **notated, presentational and autonomous**.

> [!answer]
> Texture: layered polyphony and polyrhythm vs harmony-based homophony. Dynamics: contextual vs notated. Pitch: speech-tone-influenced, variable tuning vs fixed equal temperament. Form: cyclic, open, improvisatory vs closed and through-composed. Rhythm: polyrhythm with a timeline vs metrical divisive rhythm.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Kofi Agawu (_Representing African Music_) warns against overstating the contrast: African musics also use harmony, and Western music has rhythmic complexity. Still, the **timeline-based polyrhythm** and **participatory cyclic forms** are widely recognised African hallmarks (Nketia, Arom).

## Simplified explanation

African music uses **many overlapping rhythms**, **speech-like pitches**, **repeating cycles** and is **shared by all**; Western art music uses **written harmony, fixed tuning and fixed forms**.
hint: Element by element, contrast with examples.

body: (i) Briefly discuss the **problem of the meaning of music** in the African context, with examples. (ii) Discuss why it is termed the **'musical arts of Africa'**. _(Also asked: why 'African musics' or 'the musical arts of Africa' is preferred to 'African music'.)_
answer:
**(i) The problem of meaning:**
- Many African languages **lack a single word for 'music'** in the Western sense; terms cover song, drumming, dance and play together (e.g. Akan _agorɔ_, Ewe _vu_ for drum and drumming).
- The meaning of a performance is **contextual**: the same music may mean celebration, mourning or ritual depending on occasion and participants; meaning lies in **function and social context**, not sound alone.
- **Outsider (etic) definitions** imposed by Western scholars misread African practices; insider (emic) understanding is required.
- Music is often **inseparable from language** (drum language, proverbs) and **religion**.

**(ii) Why 'musical arts of Africa' or 'African musics':**
- **Integration:** music, dance, drama, poetry, costume and visual arts are performed **together** as one event (Nzewi): no single term like 'music' captures it.
- **Diversity:** Africa has thousands of cultures and musical traditions, so the plural **'musics'** avoids implying one homogeneous 'African music'.
- It **respects indigenous conceptions** and avoids a Eurocentric category.
- E.g. an **Adowa** performance combines drumming, singing, symbolic dance gestures and kente costume as one art.

> [!answer]
> No single word for music in many languages; meaning is contextual and functional; outsider definitions mislead; music is fused with language and religion. 'Musical arts of Africa' captures the integration of music, dance, drama and visual art; 'musics' captures diversity and avoids Eurocentric homogenisation.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Meki Nzewi and the CIIMDA project popularised 'musical arts'; Kofi Agawu and others debate the concept of 'African music'. The issue reflects broader **decolonial** concerns about knowledge categories in ethnomusicology.

## Simplified explanation

Many African languages have **no word just for music**: it is mixed with dance and drama, and its meaning depends on the **occasion**. So scholars say **'musical arts of Africa'** and **'African musics'** (many kinds).

body: Discuss the concept of **Ubuntu** in participation in the musical arts of Africa, considering the circles of life: (a) birth (b) adulthood (c) death (d) ancestorship (e) reincarnation.
answer:
**Ubuntu** ('I am because we are') stresses **community, shared humanity and interdependence**. In the musical arts it shows in **communal participation**: everyone has a role, and music marks each stage of the **life cycle**, binding the individual to the community.

- **(a) Birth:** naming/outdooring ceremonies with songs and drumming welcome the child into the community; lullabies and women's songs.
- **(b) Adulthood:** puberty and initiation rites (**Dipo**, Bragoro) use songs and dances to teach adult roles and values; marriage songs; work and recreational music build social bonds; youth associations (Asafo) perform music.
- **(c) Death:** funeral music (**Adowa, Nnwonkoro, dirges**, Agbadza) expresses collective mourning, honours the dead, comforts the bereaved, and the community participates.
- **(d) Ancestorship:** music (libation songs, atumpan drum poetry, festivals such as **Akwasidae**) communicates with and venerates ancestors, maintaining the bond between the living and the dead.
- **(e) Reincarnation:** belief that ancestors return in newborns completes the cycle; songs and names at birth acknowledge the returned ancestor, linking past, present and future.

**Conclusion:** through Ubuntu, African musical arts are **participatory, life-long and communal**, affirming each person's humanity within the community across the whole cycle of life.

> [!answer]
> Ubuntu (I am because we are) frames music as communal participation marking each life stage: birth (naming songs), adulthood (initiation, marriage, work music), death (funeral dances, dirges), ancestorship (libation songs, festivals), reincarnation (birth rites honouring returning ancestors).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

The 'circle of life' model reflects the African **cyclical worldview** (Mbiti's 'living-dead'). Music is the medium of transition through rites of passage (van Gennep), with Ubuntu providing the ethical basis of participation.

## Simplified explanation

Ubuntu means 'I am because we are'. Music brings the **community together at birth, growing up, death, honouring ancestors and rebirth**.

body: Using a **named ensemble** in a specified locality, write about: (a) a brief history (b) performance practice (c) costume (d) instrumental set-up (e) occasions for performance.
answer:
**Sample: Adowa (Akan, e.g. Kumasi, Ashanti Region)**

**(a) Brief history:** Adowa ('antelope') is said to derive from the graceful movements of the **antelope**; tradition links it to a queen mother's mourning and to funeral performances among the Akan. It developed as the most popular Akan **funeral and social dance**, now performed nationally.

**(b) Performance practice:** led by the **master drummer** on the **atumpan**; a **female chorus** with a cantor sings songs (proverbs, praise, lament) in call and response; dancers (mainly women, also men) perform graceful steps with expressive **hand and body gestures** that carry meanings (e.g. pointing to the sky for God, crossing wrists for 'I am bound'); the audience participates (spraying money, joining the dance).

**(c) Costume:** for funerals, **red, black or brown** cloth (kobene, kuntunkuni); for celebrations, **kente** or white; women wrap cloth around the body with beads and headgear; men wear cloth over the left shoulder.

**(d) Instrumental set-up:** **atumpan** (master, a pair), **apentemma**, **petia**, **dawuro** (bell, timeline), **adukurogya** (castanet) and other supporting drums; the bell and supporting drums keep ostinato patterns while the atumpan improvises and cues dancers.

**(e) Occasions:** **funerals** (the main occasion), festivals (Akwasidae), durbars, installation of chiefs, weddings, national celebrations and tourism shows.

> [!answer]
> Choose an ensemble (e.g. Adowa, Kumasi) and cover history, performance practice (master drum, chorus, gestures), costume (funeral colours, kente), instruments (atumpan, apentemma, petia, dawuro) and occasions (funerals, festivals, durbars).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Alternative ensembles: **Agbadza** (Ewe, Volta: sogo, kidi, kagan, gankogui, axatse; originally a war dance, now recreational and funeral), **Kpanlogo** (Ga, Accra: 1960s youth recreational music), **Baamaaya** (Dagomba). Specificity of locality and accurate instrument names earn marks.

## Simplified explanation

Pick an ensemble you know, like **Adowa** in Kumasi, and describe its **history, how it is performed, the costumes, the drums, and when it is performed** (mainly funerals).

body: Using the movie **_Umoja_** as a source reference, discuss **four factors** that account for **change in African music**.
answer:
_Umoja_ ('unity' in Swahili), the South African stage production and film, traces the history of South African music from rural traditions to township and contemporary styles. Factors of change it illustrates:

1. **Colonialism and missionary activity:** introduced Western instruments (guitar, piano, brass), hymns and harmony, and suppressed some indigenous practices, producing choral and church-influenced styles.
2. **Urbanisation and migration:** movement to mining towns and cities (e.g. Johannesburg) created new **township** styles (marabi, kwela, mbaqanga) mixing rural traditions with urban life.
3. **Technology and mass media:** radio, recording, film and television spread new sounds, created stars and commercial genres, and connected Africa to global music (jazz, gospel, hip hop).
4. **Globalisation and cultural contact:** exposure to American jazz, gospel, pop and later hip hop led to fusion (Afro-jazz, kwaito, Afrobeats).
5. **Political struggle:** apartheid-era protest songs and freedom music, and post-independence nationalism, shaped content and styles.
6. **Economic factors and commercialisation:** music as a livelihood and industry changed performance contexts from communal to staged.

> [!answer]
> Colonialism and missions (new instruments and hymns), urbanisation and migration (township styles), technology and media (radio, recording), globalisation (jazz, hip hop fusion), political struggle (protest music), commercialisation, as dramatised in Umoja's journey from village to township to modern stage.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Music change is driven by both **internal dynamics** (creativity, generational taste) and **external contact**. Nketia distinguishes traditional, neo-traditional and popular/contemporary forms along this continuum of change.

## Simplified explanation

_Umoja_ shows African music changing because of **missionaries and colonial rule**, **moving to cities**, **radio and recordings**, **global influences** and **political struggle**.
hint: Use scenes from the film as evidence.

body: Briefly explain, with appropriate examples, the following **elements of dance**: (a) rhythm (b) space (c) movement (d) form (e) costume.
answer:
- **Rhythm:** the **pattern of timing and accents** that the dancer's movements follow or interact with, often the drum or bell **timeline** (e.g. Adowa steps on the dawuro pattern; Agbadza torso contractions on the beat).
- **Space:** **where** the dance happens: **levels** (high, middle, low: crouching in Atsiagbekor), **directions**, **pathways** (circles, lines), **size** of movement, and the performance area (arena, stage).
- **Movement:** **what** the body does: locomotor (walking, leaping) and non-locomotor (bending, twisting, shoulder shaking) actions and **gestures** with meaning (Adowa hand signs, Kete steps).
- **Form:** the **structure or organisation** of the dance: opening, development, climax and close; sections, repetition and variation; solo, duet or group formations (e.g. Bamaaya's progression of sections).
- **Costume:** the **clothing and accessories** worn: they identify roles and culture, enhance movement and carry symbolism (e.g. Bamaaya skirts and waist rattles; Kete kente; funeral colours in Adowa).

> [!answer]
> Rhythm = timing pattern following the drums or timeline; space = levels, directions, pathways, area; movement = locomotor and non-locomotor actions and gestures; form = structure and organisation; costume = clothing that identifies and symbolises.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

These elements overlap with the general **BASTE** framework (body, action, space, time, energy). African dance adds **polycentric** movement (several body parts moving to different rhythms) and **symbolic gesture**.

## Simplified explanation

Dance has **rhythm** (timing), **space** (where), **movement** (what the body does), **form** (structure) and **costume** (what is worn), e.g. Adowa's graceful hand signs to the drums.
hint: Define each and give a Ghanaian dance example.

body: (a) Discuss the **nature versus nurture** schools of thought in relation to musical learning in Africa. (b) Explain in detail how the **apprenticeship model** works with Albert Bandura's **social learning theory**.
answer:
**(a) Nature vs nurture**
- **Nature:** musical ability is **innate/inherited**: some people are 'born' musicians; in some African societies music is a **hereditary occupation** (griots/jelis of Mande society; royal drummers' lineages among the Akan), suggesting talent runs in families.
- **Nurture:** musical ability is **learned** through the **environment**: in Africa, children are **immersed** in music from birth (lullabies, play songs, festivals), learn through participation, observation and practice, so most people become competent participants.
- **Synthesis:** both interact: potential may be inborn, but the **communal, participatory environment** develops it (John Blacking, _How Musical is Man?_, on the Venda: 'all normal people are musical').

**(b) Apprenticeship with Bandura's social learning theory**
Bandura holds that people learn by **observing models** through four processes:
1. **Attention:** the apprentice watches the **master** drummer, singer or dancer closely during rehearsals and real performances.
2. **Retention:** they **memorise** patterns, songs and drum language, often aided by **mnemonics/vocables** and repetition (oral transmission).
3. **Reproduction:** they **practise and imitate**, starting with simple supporting parts (bell, rattle, supporting drums) and progressing to the master drum.
4. **Motivation/reinforcement:** praise, correction, social recognition, money gifts and the prospect of becoming a master motivate learning.

In the African apprenticeship model, learning is **situated** in community life, **long-term**, **hierarchical** (respect for the master), **oral and aural**, and gradual, a clear application of observational learning and **modelling**.

> [!answer]
> Nature: innate, hereditary talent (griots, royal drummer families). Nurture: learning through immersion and participation; both interact (Blacking). Apprenticeship applies Bandura's attention, retention, reproduction and motivation: watch the master, memorise orally, practise from simple to master parts, and be motivated by praise and recognition.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Bandura's **modelling** and **self-efficacy** concepts explain why apprentices progress when they see peers and masters succeed. Lave and Wenger's 'legitimate peripheral participation' similarly describes how novices move from the periphery to full membership of a community of practice.

## Simplified explanation

Some say musicians are **born**; others say they are **made** by growing up surrounded by music: both matter. Apprentices learn by **watching the master, remembering, practising and being encouraged**, which is Bandura's theory.
